utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam, registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First of all, I would like to inform the parties that due to health reasons Witness 69 will not testify, certainly not viva voce, this week. You will receive further information. Then, Mr. Cayley, are you ready to continue your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: May it please, Your Honours. Thank you. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps, Mr. Ermolaev, before I allow Mr. Cayley to continue, I would like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony. Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Ermolaev, good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If, please, the court officer could bring up Exhibit D50?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Ermolaev, just to orientate you on this document, it is a request for information from the deputy minister of the interior of the Republic of Croatia to a number of police administrations in Croatia including, you can see there, Zadar, Knin, and Knin [sic]. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we could just go over the page, please. The date of the document just to be clear is August 22, 1995. Do you see that? Did you see that?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I saw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, if you could just read that through. Mr. Ermolaev, if you could just let me know when you've finished reading that page and I'll move it to the next page for you.

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, number 4, the last one that I finished, "The above cited cases..."

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes, so I'll move it to the next page for you so you can read the whole document. If the next page, please, could be brought up. You'll be glad here is a shorter page. If the -- if the document could be brought back to the first page and just one preliminary question. You're happy, are you, Mr. Ermolaev? You've read it?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes. From what you can see in that document it's broadly dealing with operational police matters, yes?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, if you look at the front of the document, you'll see that it's from the deputy minister of the interior to various police administrations. Now, for your information, and it's not disputed in this case, at this time the head of the police administration in Zadar-Knin was a man called Mr. Cetina, and the head of the police administration in Knin was a man called Cedo Romanic. Did you know either of those two gentlemen [inaudible]?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And you'll note that Mr. Cermak is not copied on this document at all, is he?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: He's not copied, is he?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I just see it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And if he had been in the chain of command somewhere between the deputy minister of interior and these chiefs of police administration you would have expect him to have been copied on such a document, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. That calls for speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can I answer that, Your Honour. I don't think so because the witness actually gave evidence pursuant to questions that Your Honour put in which he said that Mr. Cermak had operational control of the police. This is an operational document. You would have expected Mr. Cermak to have been copied on it if that was in fact true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You can ask about standard routine and procedures, whether that included copying Mr. Cermak. What one would expect depends on what usually was done and what that person was aware of what was usually done. So therefore under these circumstances in view of your knowledge of the position of Mr. Cermak, would you consider it within I would say ordinary routine that you would copy Mr. Cermak on these matters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So if not regarding, you know, such particular document in general at least as I understand it, that at least to the best of my knowledge. So when we have federal ministers and they have their branches in different territories, there is no doubt that they keep being with the control and command to the minister, and at the same time we do know that police as well is under control and guiding from the governing person who is in charge, who is the head on this particular territory. This general that I can just say about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's move on. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you gave evidence yesterday that you met Mr. Cermak, I think, on one occasion. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And it's fair to say isn't it that General Forand dealt with Mr. Cermak on a fairly regular basis as far as you can recall, yes?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At least all -- everything, because we kept close cooperation on operations level and as well between myself and Forand and Leslie. So that's why on regular basis we exchanged opinions on the situation on the ground and if needed -- so we worked out, and he kept regular contact with the Cermak office, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could have, please, Exhibit 1856 brought up. I'm sorry that's the 65 ter number. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: This, Mr. Ermolaev, is a letter from General Forand to General Ante Gotovina, and the particular passage that I'm interested in is on the second page.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we could move, please, to the second page.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And if you could please read the one, two, three, fourth paragraph on that page. And for completeness you might also wish to read the next paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ermolaev, do you recall this episode, the theft of the UN equipment?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you mean with --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think it was digging equipment. It was heavy plant equipment that was stolen at an early stage after Knin fell. Do you recall that event?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I -- I generally remember that then we experienced problems with stealing UN equipment on battalions as well as -- I mean, my UNMOs, but particularly what was stolen from battalions were never [indiscernible], just never control it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And you see that in essence General Forand is stating that General Cermak was frustrated to find that his authority was limited in assisting in essentially recovering the -- I have to be careful in how I express this. But General Cermak that his authority was limited in terms of assisting a joint investigation by the UN and HV military police to recover this equipment. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Were you aware of General Forand's opinion on this matter regarding Cermak?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all at least as I understand that was purely battalions relations with what happened to them on 24th August with KenBat vehicles or I -- I just cannot read everything here. As a rule, with the battalions' activities and activities of UNMOs usually we never exchanged, you know, such information, because actually, I mean, UN battalion commander, so it's an independent body, and so he has his own headquarters. I had my own. It so turned out that our headquarters were together in such particular mission. Usually in other missions we have separate, you know, headquarters and we just, you know, support just relations by visiting each other if needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So you're not familiar with this particular episode?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not particularly acquainted with battalions' activities, their problems, and relations between battalion commanders Forand and his reaction to the Croatian authorities at that particular moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Okay. Fine. We'll move on. Thank you. If I could ask for that to be marked for identification, please, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D150.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D150 is admitted into evidence. Mr. Cayley, if you could give me on yesterday's transcript the page and the line where the witness said that Mr. Cermak had operational control over the police. So not control over check-points or -- but operational control over the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Page 33 of the draft transcript, lines 8 to 11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: One last area, Mr. Ermolaev, and then I will be finished with you for the day. You were trying to recall the name of an individual yesterday, the principal human -- I think he was known as the PHAC, the senior UN civil servant, Mr. Al-Alfi. Do you remember Mr. Al-Alfi?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I mean visually something vague, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And he was the senior UN civil servant within Knin, yes?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If that's the right description.

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And he had a reporting chain to Zagreb like you, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's a separate structure. The United Nations for sure he had his own command and he reported his own information, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And were you aware at the time that he was actually reporting directly to the office of the special representative of the Secretary-General?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because actually, I mean, after Op Storm, and I just remember to that morning, I couldn't sleep with -- your answer when Akashi arrived where I was. And then it turned back that I was there, I just simply --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I see you --

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- cannot remember so, you know, quickly, you know, yeah. I anticipate when Akashi arrived and he gave us this new functions and results of negotiations. But in any case, with this, yes. At least as I remember, our civil affairs they became the central focus of -- of all activities, and we repeatedly met with him and discussed it, and human rights and everything, it was two maybe focus point. I mean, maybe even three. So we worked for all three structures just trying to do what they asked us to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could we please have Exhibit D56.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you'll see on this document, and I won't ask you to read all of it, but it's a report from Mr. Al-Alfi to Paavko [sic] Pitkanen at UNCRO headquarters in Zagreb and it's dated the 18th of August, 1995. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. His chain of command, yes, I see it. HQ Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If, please, we could go to 3603. It's the last page of the document. And if you could read from numeral 2 down to the end of the second paragraph, please, Mr. Ermolaev.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And maybe that could be enlarged, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've read to UNPF headquarters level.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Ah. You've read to the bottom of the page?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, UNPF headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I'm only interested actually the second paragraph, and you can see in that paragraph that the individuals present in the meeting, actually you can see the individuals present in the first part of the meeting and then in the first paragraph on that page, and then in the second paragraph you can see that Mr. Al-Alfi says that he brings to General Cermak his concerns about looting and burning. You see that, yes?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And you can also see that he states in essence that Mr. Cermak shared the concern over this issue and expressed his unhappiness; yes?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And you can see that he promises to take tough action and give some kind of explanation as to why these events are taking place, yes?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And this is all on the 18th of August, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 18th of August; right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we could please have P94, which is your statement. And if we could please go to page 9 of the statement. And what I'm interested in here, Mr. Ermolaev -- do you have that in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now if you go to the one, two, three, the fourth paragraph where you say in your statement: "What made Cermak to admit in September 1995 that arson and looting took place in the territory of the former RSK? "He kept denying everything till then."

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: So you want when I command?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: No. I mean I have a question for you.

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You were not aware of this meeting that had taken place on the 18th of August --

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: -- were you?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. So it's a little bit obvious to me. So I mean we're not now asking me. So my eye witnesses is as follows: So we have a document here and yesterday we discussed it, when in the beginning of September General Cermak officially informed there are no looting and or burning and everything okay in Sector South. That was an official protest letter from Croatian governmental authority, and where we yesterday we just read it where he said that I would be -- "And I'm astonished to hear that it's going on in the sector." So to my mind at the beginning of September whenever there is, let me say, internal reports between UNMOs what somebody send -- send a note, we have an official statement signed by the person in charge from the government of Croatia about his assessment of the situation, and if we receive in written form such a challenging answer which we all read yesterday, what direction do you expect to get from me?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: But your statement is not right, is it? He wasn't denying everything until September, was he?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. The witness has not said whether or not he was aware of the meeting in which this admission was made by General Cermak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Nevertheless, his statement is not with this reservation that to his knowledge. But I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: We can move on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think we see --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: -- Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- a letter here which apparently -- a report here describing a meeting in which the witness apparently did not take part, and the witness points at another source for his statement. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If, please, we could have 65 ter 4135 brought up.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you can see that this is another report from Mr. Al-Alfi of the 24th of August of 1995. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And you can see, I think, in the first paragraph that this is referencing a meeting at 1.30 on the 24th of August of 1995. General Forand is meeting with General Cermak. You see that, yes?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we could please go to the next page. And if you could please read paragraph 5.

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. "Cermak gave strict orders to the civilians and military personnel to stop such violations." Yes, I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, one simple question. I'm not going to ask you on the content. You were not aware of this meeting taking place, were you?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I yesterday informed that from 17th to my regret 25th August I was on my CTO days in Zadar. I think that if I was there I would have participated, no doubt about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: In this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: For sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If, please, we could now have Exhibit P94 -- actually, prior to that, I'm sorry, Your Honour. If that document could be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit 151.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That would be D151.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: D, D.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, D 151 is admitted into he have. Mr. Cayley, I've tried to find your reference to page 33. I only have the now correct transcript. I tried to reconstruct that but still couldn't find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I will, if you wish Your Honours, just so you know -- I'll photocopy it during the break and then give it to your legal officer and then you can have a look at it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: We have a copy here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed. I'll read meanwhile.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes. If, please, we could have Exhibit P94 brought up.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. Ermolaev, if you'd just go to page 6 of your statement. I just want to try and get through this as quickly as possible, so I won't bring this statement -- ah, okay. We have it now. Yeah. And the section that I'm interested in is the one, two, three, four -- the fifth paragraph where it begins --

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: "This sounded."

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: "On 7 September." It's the second sentence of that paragraph --

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: -- that you've got. Do you see it?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found it. Yeah, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And you recall that that protest letter was signed by General Forand to Mr. Cermak, yes?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at least as it is stated here that was supposed to be sent by General Forand, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If, please, we could now have 65 ter -- oh, I'm sorry, P38, actually. It has an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And you can see that this is a report again from Mr. Al-Alfi, dated the 8th of September to UNCRO headquarters in Zagreb, yes?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And if, please, we could go to page 3 of that document. And I'm interested in the first four lines of the second paragraph. Can you read that all right, Mr. Ermolaev? It's at a slight angle.

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And you see that the meeting between Mr. Cermak and the PHAC was held actually on the same day as the letter that you refer to in your statement from General Forand complaining about criminal activity, yes?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I -- well, yes. On 7 September, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And you can also see that the deputy sector commander participated in that meeting. That was General Forand's deputy, yes?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And if you could now go, please, to the next paragraph which begins "During ..."

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I read this paragraph, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Okay. You were back from Zadar by now, yes?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: But you were not aware of this meeting taking place either?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean by "either"?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Were you aware of what took place at this particular meeting?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: So -- so practically the system as I mentioned --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes. I understand the reporting mechanisms. It's really a simple question. Were you aware of what took place at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: We -- we -- we usually, you know, just discuss it and each branch had its own meeting and its own responsibilities, so that's why -- I mean, this particular meeting maybe just when we discuss it with Forand, maybe he regarded to this meeting as well, but I do not clearly remember that on 17th, because I remember the whole day we were preparing the answer to General Cermak letter, and this was not in the focus of attention, this meeting, and what was said there, because we will prepare an official report on -- you know, a government letter. So I do not quite recall. I received information from -- from him about his meetings, what they discussed, but I cannot particularly -- because the 7th September came down in my memory as a flash of the answer that was prepared and that we did to be able to properly answer the questions raised in Cermak's letter, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask one additional question in relation to this document. The last line of the paragraph you've just read is: "General Cermak agreed to give his instructions for more joint patrolling between UNCIVPOL and the Croatian police, particularly in the remote villages." Do you have any knowledge about joint UNCIVPOL and Croatian police patrols at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I cannot say when really, but, I mean, you know, after some time being I cannot set exact date, but I do confirm that United Nations Civilian Police. So if there was some concerns we informed their structures, and they were in close cooperation with their Croatian colleagues, and they conducted joint patrollings, that's for sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you give us any indication as to the frequency or intensity of joint patrolling?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, no. I cannot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I don't have any further questions. Thank you, Mr. Ermolaev.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley, before we continue you gave me page 33. I'm not a native English speaker. You said that you did put the question to the witness, and you said that in response to an objection raised by Mr. Russo because the witness testified yesterday that he was -- I think you used the word "operational control of the police." What I see, however, on page 33 is that the witness said that the main roads and all operations of Croatian police was under his direct command. Now, command and control is, for good reasons, always used as a -- two different things. So therefore, I was -- I'd prefer you always to specifically quote what the witness said rather than to give your own interpretation, because operational control and operational command is not exactly the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then who is next in line? Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just need to use the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The lectern for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ermolaev, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Kuzmanovic, who is counsel for Mr. Markac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Ermolaev.

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ermolaev, in several of the sitreps the term "bombreps" is used. Can you tell us what that means?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I just have a look from the context?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Could we pull up P102, please. Page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: At the very bottom under "Reports from KenBat." "There were a total of 1230 bombreps," and then in parentheses, "(638 ARSK, 592 HV/HVO)." I'm reading that, and this is a sitrep dated August 4, 1995, which was released by you. What is a bombrep?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, it was released by me. I'm just turning back to my eye witnessing and the precision. So this report by battalions which exclusively for these days, when we exchanged information. So typically I mean we just did not use bombardment report. We use, you know, just artillery shellings or arty shell or some firing rep -- firerep, but Canadians they use bombrep. So I just.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. In this case it was the Kenyans. KenBat is Kenyans?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kenyans okay. Kenyans okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: So bombrep would mean essentially artillery --

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to me yes. To me yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Would be artillery?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they have their specifications. Better to consult with them. So I think as bombrep, bombardment report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay so at least --

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: To me, I mean we had just firing report, fire reps we calls them. Maybe they're not equal I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, at least according to this document this sitrep of the 4th of August which is the first day of Operation Storm; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: The report from KenBat is that there were -- there was at least more bombreps from the ARSK side than there was from the HV/HVO side; correct? Mr. Ermolaev, let me just --

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I see. 63 -- 63 P -- yeah, I just see. There were a total of 1230 bombreps; yes? Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And at least KenBat in this report, not to belabour it, actually counted the bombreps and found that the ARSK had 638 and the HV/HVO had 592; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: The first page of the sitrep of 4 August 1995, Mr. Ermolaev, if we could go to the first page, please. If we could focus on highlight number 1. The second paragraph of highlight number 1 says: "RSK authorities requested UN to assist in evacuation of approximately 32.000 civ population from N. Dalmatian Corps AOR." So in your mind when you put this report together and released it, Mr. Ermolaev, was it your understanding that the RSK authorities were asking the UN to help evacuate 32.000 civilians from the area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: So it's a little bit -- I don't understand, I mean, your question. Can you just rephrase it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Was it your understanding that the RSK was asking the United Nations to evacuate 32.000 civilians from the area of responsibility? This is your report, Mr. Ermolaev, released by you.

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was released by me. It states that we had a meeting with local authorities after the heavy shellings which took place the whole day, and when even united --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Ermolaev. It doesn't say that. It says "RSK authorities requested UN to assist in evacuation --"

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] so why should I comment it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: What did you do?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't do anything. We just informed in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Ermolaev, you said in your statement, which is P94 -- actually, we'll go to P95. I'm sorry. Paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: "I personally reviewed and released all daily and update sitreps." Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: So this was a sitrep of the 4th of August, the first day of Operation Storm that you personally had released; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, is it true, Mr. Ermolaev -- we'll go to P94. Page 8. Could we go to page 8 of P94, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If the witness has a hard copy, we can continue even before it's on the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ermolaev, do you have a hard copy?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Thank you, Your Honour. In the second paragraph that begins, "I do not remember," I'd like you to go down to the third last sentence which starts "I can," and I will read it. "I can add that all highlights in all sitreps were written personally by me." Did you find that, Mr. Ermolaev?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I found it. Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And going back to the sitrep of the 4th of August, 1995, which was P102, the commentary regarding the evacuation request for the civilian population was listed as a highlight; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'd like you to go to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, please, to P104. And when we get to P104, first page, this is a sitrep dated -- update, dated the 5th of August at 0400 Bravo, that's 4.00 in the morning, correct, Mr. Ermolaev?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: In August of 1995. And in the paragraph that begins "In the evening of 4 August," I'd like the registrar to please go to the section that begins "from the early morning" and highlight that, please. "From the early morning CA, Croatian army -- arty," and I'm assuming that's artillery, "shelled various Krajina towns, especially targeting barracks. The goal of the offensive is to take the whole Krajina." Did I read that correctly?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: This was your sitrep; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was sitrep issued by UNMO Sector South at that particular time, yes. I do confirm it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And then on page 2 of that document, P104, at the very top "KenBat reported," and KenBat is the Kenyan Battalion that we mentioned earlier; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: The second notation under "KenBat" was beginning on the second line of the second notation: "There was an exchange of HMG and arty fire from both sides of the WFs." WFs meaning warring factions; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely correct. Yes. I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Underneath the JordBat-3 section, about halfway in, the Jordanian battalion reports at about 2235 Bravo, meaning in the evening; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: "Hundred of vehicles were reported heading BiH," and BiH is Bosnia; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: "The vehicles are mostly from Gracac, Knin, and Udbina." Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: So people were already leaving for Bosnia as of the 4th of August in the evening; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, generally -- well, what I just remember that starting from 2022, I mean, military and civilians, they started departing Krajina area, yes. I know about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'd like the registrar to please move on to P -- sorry, Your Honour. We just recently got these P numbers, and with the dossier I'm a little slow at getting the particular exhibit number. Actually, this is D124.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can't blame anyone for having received that number late.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: This is another sitrep, the 5th of August, day two of Operation Storm. Correct, Mr. Ermolaev? Actually, it's not the same document that I have. Could the registrar please pull up 65 ter 4696. Is that the same -- is it the same document? Okay. Thank you. It's different from the -- can we try an ERN number? R --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you move up just a tiny little bit then you'll see that D124 is R0642981, which is exactly the same number as we see on the screen. I take it that you pulled that up as 65 --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I have a different ERN number --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- under the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I have a different ERN number, Your Honour. I think that was problem. And I will give the registrar the ERN number. It's R0642991 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's an eight-page document. Let me just see how far it goes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mine is only three pages, at least from the dossier I received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The D124 appears to me to be an eight-page document --

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- but the last two digits are 88. Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe he's looking for Exhibit P105.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thanks for your patience.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Ermolaev -- thank you for pulling that up for us, Madam Registrar. This is another the sitrep update dated 5 August of 1995, and I'd like you to go to page 2, please. The Jordanian battalion is reporting in its second note "Exchange of artillery fire by both of the warring factions ongoing." And in the middle of their report the Jordanians note that 137 vehicles were reported crossing from RSK to BiH. Later in that same paragraph, "203 vehicles in addition to 2.000 refugees were reported crossing borders to BiH." I read that correctly, did I not?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just to have this clear, this kind of report, you're reporting about vehicles, is this mainly civilian vehicles or --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So as a rule battalions they have the same procedure of reporting. If they were military, let me say, and identification, kinds, and et cetera. They would have mentioned it that these vehicles -- or anything that is moving, I mean, with military purpose, then they would indicate. So out of the stacks. So it's clear that these are exclusively civilian cars, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And I'll demonstrate the difference in the next exhibit, P108, page 1. At the bottom of page 1, again the Jordanian battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And your recollection is, Mr. Ermolaev, is that the Jordanian battalion was close to the border between Croatia. Its area of responsibility was -- included the border between Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina, did it not?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, vaguely, yes. You reminded me. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Again this time the Jordanian battalion reports in this exhibit, P108 --

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: -- "10 ARSK tanks followed by 200 soldiers with their individual weapons were reported heading Bosnia."

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: "One tank remained deployed in the area and aiming towards JordBat 3 position." Did I read that correctly? Meaning JordBat 3 position going on to the following page.

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: HV soldiers with tremendous around the P -- what this?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: The Jordanians were specific over distinguishing between military and civilian vehicles, were they not, Mr. Ermolaev?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have another page about -- on the screen. "45 HV soldiers in addition to mine destroyer and an APC were reported around the OP."

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's the next entry, correct? That's the following entry from the one that I had read?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, JordBat's reposition. Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I'd like to move to P109, please. First page. This is also something that was released by you, Mr. Ermolaev, on the 6th of August of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: The fourth page of this document -- actually, the fifth page of this document. Now, I'll read the section B at the bottom. "UNMO team Gracac reported." "UNMO team met with commander of HV special forces and allowed to carry out patrol in Gracac." So this is August 6th the UNMO team in Gracac essentially has freedom of movement; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, absolutely not correct. I mean, that doesn't clearly indicate the system. I mean, the system of patrolling and everything we just establish with governor Cermak. That was, you know, initiative and good relations between UNMOs and Croatian forces there that particular day, but that was not the system.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, this is August 6th. I'm not talking about any time General Cermak came into Knin. This is August 6th on day two of Operation Storm, the UNMO team Gracac is reporting that they are allowed to carry out a patrol in Gracac; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In -- in some particular case. In this particular minute that it took place, yes, but it was not the system, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic, just let's try to get to the core. I mean, if you are allowed to come to this courtroom, does that mean that you have freedom of movement in these UN premises? I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I think I made my point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At least certain places I would expect not to see you. Cafeteria, fine. Defence counsel room, fine. But let's try to -- I mean, we -- the Chamber can read --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and the Chamber is -- it does not escape our attention if by this way of putting words on an equal footing where they could easily be understood not to be the same that -- that doesn't escape our attention it. I just wanted you to know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ermolaev, you aware that the Sarinic-Akashi agreement had yet to be signed as of the time that this patrol was in Gracac?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: So I'm sorry, but I -- I was not informed about the conscious plannings for agreements and negotiations between United Nations authorities and governmental authorities of Croatia. That was not my level just to know about it. So that's why I mean for us till the time you get an order that your function is finished, so we continued to carry out and implement very important system and activities we had as we have it till the time we get, Please stop it, and that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: My question used -- was fairly simple, Mr. Ermolaev.

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: The Akashi-Sarinic agreement was what set forth the parameters as to how the UN would operate in Croatia after the initiation of Operation Storm. That's correct, isn't it? I mean, that's how you were operating as UNMOs.

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was informed about it from Mr. Akashi on the -- on the day of his arrival, and, yes. But till that time I hadn't known about it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Could we please go to P111. Mr. Ermolaev, are you aware that, and you can tell me if you're not, that Gracac was an important crossroads in terms of going from north to south, east to west?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If we could go to page 3, in the middle of the paragraph. "UNMO team Gracac reported." "UNMO team enjoyed freedom of movement between Gracac and Gospic. UNMO team discovered that the main arty (HV) impacts was around main junction. Arty shell missed UNMO house by 50 metres." Did I read that correctly?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: P117, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we move on, I see in this -- this same sitrep, Mr. Ermolaev, lines like "UNMO team was stopped at junction Bruyno by HV special forces. They informed UNMO that operation is still on." If it is reported that you had freedom of movement between Gracac and Gospic, what does that actually mean, that you are allowed to move between Gracac and Gospic, or that you're allowed to freely move in the whole of the area and -- I'll first perhaps ask you these questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, so to me it's obvious that we could not have any just even think about to my understanding about freedom of movement when we were blocked in headquarters Sector South, the main bulk of UNMOs there. So just to explain why and whether we can assess from our point of view the fact that we have in Gracac that my UNMOs managed going out of the house and see Croatian forces, different kinds, different types, and speak to them. So my assessment is -- I mean, it's typical for anyone working in such conditions. The Croatian units which met our UNMOs, they didn't have any instruction and anything. So they know UNMOs because we had half of our forces, I mean United Nations observers, were on the territory of Croatian side, and they know that United Nations military observers, they monitor the areas. So -- and I can imagine that they just arrived there in the area because they were not yet, you know -- because there were absolutely different taskings at that particular moment, at least as I assess it. And that's why they didn't have any restrictions of movement received from high command that you should not deny access of UNMOs or whatever. So my explanations to this fact is yes, that we were very happy that we received that at least, you know, some teams and such days managed to go out to speak, to clarify situation on the ground. That was the main aim. But to speak about freedom of movement as we understand it in accordance with the agreement signed between the United Nations and government of Croatia. So it -- it has absolutely no connections, I mean, to my understanding. I mean, this is the fact that we had such an episode, and I -- I never expected, frankly speaking, that after reintegration we will experience such, you know, severe restrictions of movements, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Although this was a rather lengthy answer, Mr. Kuzmanovic, it might not be a very direct response to my question. It appears to me that when we're talking about freedom of movement that if the basic position is that you've got freedom of movement that whatever report there is that you have freedom of movement in A or in B or on the road between A and B, you can look at it from two different angles. The one is that at least you could move from A to B or you could move in A, or you to move in B, but of course the other approach would be that you are limited and not had freedom of movement in the whole of the area. So that's the first issue. What does freedom of movement mean? The second is if there are limitations, for what reasons. And the third question, and I remember that there was one agreement that who decides whether the reasons for the limitations are applicable, and what is the procedure so as who consults whom before of a decision is taken. I think these are the core questions as far as freedom of movement is concerned, and I do not know then whether -- I just want you to know that that is on my mind, and if I see such a document that you should not be surprised that I look at from the different angles.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Sure, I understand that, Your Honour. I think it's pretty clear that since this report of the 7th of August was released by Mr. Ermolaev, that had there been any qualifications those would have been included in the rather lengthy sitrep of this date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: This is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- some of them aren't isn't it. That's exactly what I'm drawing your attention to if there are any qualifications. If you say you've got -- let's take this building again. If you say, "You've got freedom of movement from the cafeteria to the Defence counsel's room," then again you could say, "That's fine. I can move freely around this building." And of course the other approach is that you're really strictly limited from going to this place to that place on this premises. And therefore I just want to let you know that you're putting of course the questions very much in see there was freedom of movement in the line next to the one where it says that there is no freedom of movement and people were blocked, et cetera, but that it has two sides this coin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, certainly, Your Honour. I think that the earlier -- the earlier notation on this sitrep on the same page saying that the UN team was stopped at Junction Bruyno, as Your Honour said, by special forces. I mean that's pretty clear. It's a specific issue that obviously limited freedom of movement, but there were no such qualifications or limitations on the section related to Gracac and that's why I wanted to point that out to the Chamber and obviously talk to the witness about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, are you -- let's then explore that. Between Gracac and Gospic is that municipalities or cities or -- and why doesn't it say in the whole of the whole of the municipality of Gracac. Why is it between? Between suggests a line connecting to two items.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ermolaev, there's a significant road that goes between Gracac and Gospic, does it not?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I -- I do not remember exactly now, but, yes, there's a road there. So -- and here we have, you know, grid reference, if I understand it correctly now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, at least on the --

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Junction, yeah. So I mean we -- we could, I mean, just find out. But in any case, I mean, that significant road, yes. So my answer yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of whether or not the Special Police of the Ministry of the Interior were the forces that were essentially covering the ground at Gracac and were the leading spearhead of that activity?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether or not General Markac informed the UNMO on the 7th of August in Gracac of what he was doing and where he was going?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly. I just only -- just something vaguely, you mentioned this name, because it's -- I can't remember exactly, but something I remember, but not so much specifically. Okay. So far.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Who was the UNMO team Gracac, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember, you know, the names, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: How many people? I know it's hard to remember, but --

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know, I had too many, you know, people, you know, under my command, so I cannot remember everywhere. But I do believe that with all CTOs, leaves, and et cetera, there might have been maybe 4, plus minus. I can be mistaken now. But we can -- I mean, we've made all results of those UN personnel for the security reasons those who were there on the Croatian side and some -- and on this side, on the former RSK territory, right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ermolaev, you have a tendency of not only sincerely trying to answer the question but also to give some explanation, some further explore the matter that was in the question. May I ask you to very much focus to answer the questions, first of all.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'd like to move on to P117, please. I'd like to go to the second page of that document. In the middle of the page where it says: "At D. Polijce check-point." P117, just for reference, is a sitrep dated the 12th it of August of 1995, and in that sitrep there's a notation that "The platoon commander told UNMOs 5.000 RSK refugees passed through that point toward Drvar BiH." He also stated that there was one brig --" brigade, is that what that means?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: "... deployed around the AOR with six --"

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: "-- tanks inside BH territory." Now, the following paragraph discusses at second Sekanivrsak, I probably mispronounced that and I apologise, we were informed that 71.200 refugees used that check-point towards Banja Luka, most of them came from Knin. Where did you get -- oh, sorry. From whom was that number received? The number of 71.200.

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my regret I cannot just comment on this UNMO team now at this particular minute. I mean, more towards the source. I see here something is --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Maybe I'll re-ask the question. Upon what basis, if you know, are these numbers reported? What is the source?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. Well, the main source, at least as I understand, was that when we had some, for example, civilians or as we saw in report by battalions when they observed some movement and they report the number if they see it. So generally about refugees, at least as I remember. So that the main sources, as I mentioned, was physical seeing of such an event. Secondly, if information was told by someone. I mean, by local population, by Croatian side, by liaison officers. Thirdly, we received as well information from different other United Nations organisations --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ermolaev --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From ICRC, human rights --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. A number appears in a report saying, "We were informed that 71.200 refugees used that check point." Now, Mr. Kuzmanovic would like to know what this specific number is based. Now you start explaining to us what in general your sources of information were, but --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, I -- I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would gladly accept that but that's not what Mr. Kuzmanovic is trying to find out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, okay. So I do not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you know or do you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That could have been a shorter answer. Please proceed, Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. We'll proceed in such ways. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ermolaev, can you direct us, or the Chamber, or anyone to determine how that number or who we can find out from whom that number is reached?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do believe that it's very easy to be done. I mean, those UNMOs who reported they might remember where this figure came from.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: So your advice is to go to the UNMO Gospic, whoever they were, at the time of this report of August 12th of 1995?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic, I think we're not asking the witness advice specifically. At least that's not what we should do. What we should do is ask for what the witness knows, what he observed, what information he could give to us, and then it apparently here he has some difficulties in leading us to the source.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'll move on. Thank you. Given the time, Your Honour, would you like me to continue with the next theme or break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It depends. If your next subject could be dealt within not more than three to eight minutes, then it's fine. Otherwise, it would be time for a break now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I will not be done in three to eight minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we'll have a break now. We'll resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. -- I don't know who I have to address, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly, it's you which will address the matter which I just wanted to announce, that is, that the Chamber was informed that the Prosecution would like to make an oral application for a -- for a testimony through videolink, and we'll deal with that in private session for the time being. So can we move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, for the Chamber's notice I have one general area to cover and then I should be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ermolaev, one of your colleagues, UNMO colleagues, was a man by the name of Alexander Tchernetsky; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And he was during the time of and after Operation Storm was on Team Podkonje, was he not?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, could you please pull up 3D00089. It's a statement of Mr. Tchernetsky dated May 18, 2002. And with the assistance of the usher I'd like to get a copy of that statement to Mr. Ermolaev.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ermolaev, I'd like you to turn to page 4 of Mr. Tchernetsky's statement, please. And let me know when you're there?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: The bottom of page 4. Before I get to that, you in your statement, Mr. Ermolaev, noted for us in P94, on page 3, that the new duties of the UNMOs, which included monitoring and reporting on human rights, carrying out surveillance, designating two UNMOs for HRAT activity, and assistance in providing civilian population with humanitarian needs and monitoring the general situation, that was within the mandate of the UNMOs at least as of your understanding; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: We'll go back to --

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can we just -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Can we please go back to the Tchernetsky statement now again, page 4. At the bottom of page 4, and it goes into page 5, states: "Approximately on 24-25 August 1995 during the patrol to the region of Podinarje I found a small hamlet between Bukvin Stan and Musica Stanovi where remained several elderly Serbian families. I got information from the residents that several RSK soldiers were hiding," I'm going to the top of page 5, "in the woods. With the help of the of civilians I met two of the soldiers and spoke to them. Firstly, I decided not to report to the HQ about the soldiers and only reported about civilians in order to organise the humanitarian aid for them." And I'll stop there for a moment. Now, Mr. Ermolaev, it's true, is it not, that in the sitreps of August 24th, 25th, through the 28th, the UNMO Team Podkonje did not make any report about civilians in this region mentioned in the Tchernetsky statement to organise humanitarian aid.

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we could have a look --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- daily sitreps for these days, because I was in Zadar with this. Just to remind me a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: We'll go to the 24th, which is 65 ter 4712. And if we could go to the fourth page of that document.

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Under section D, ii, "UNMO Team Podkonje." It says what it says. There's no mention in that section of the civilians in order to organise humanitarian aid; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. 24th, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move, then, to the 25th, which is 65 ter 4713. And if we can go to the third page. Under section H, "Team Podkonje reported." Again, no mention of reporting civilians in order to organise humanitarian aid for them; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. No, Podinarje right now. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Then if we can go to 65 ter 4146, which is the 26th of August. And you can correct me if I'm wrong, but on section E, which is one, two, three, four -- the fifth page, there is no mention again of Bukvin Stan and Musica Stanovi humanitarian assistance; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't see here in the report, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And then if we go to the 27th of August, which is 65 ter 4714 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic, are these all outside the range of the sitreps that were [overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: They are not, Your Honour. They are exhibits, unfortunately I don't have them matched up in my book answer as exhibits, and I will go back and correct the record for that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know whether the record can correct it for those purposes, because of course what you said in court is a reference to the 65 ter numbers which makes it almost impossible to -- to correct the record, and it's very difficult for those who will consult the record at a later stage to find the proper exhibit numbers which, as Madam Registrar tells me, are P126, P127, and P128.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I have the references now, Your Honour. Thank you. The August 27th sitrep is P129, Your Honour. And on page 2 of P129, under section (h), "UNMO Team Podkonje ..." Again, Mr. Tchernetsky's assertion in the statement that they reported about civilians in order to organise humanitarian aid is not contained in the report; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And we move to the sitrep dated August 28th, 1995, which is P130. This sitrep discusses the hand-over of the former RSK soldiers, does it not, Mr. Ermolaev?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, clearly stated, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And it's a report that was released by you; right?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Before going into the details of P130, I would like to go back to Mr. Tchernetsky's statement, which is 3D00089. Page 5. To the top of page 5, please. Now, Mr. Ermolaev, to be clear, we went through the daily sitreps from the 24th to the 27th of August, and Mr. Tchernetsky's statement about reporting civilians in order to organise humanitarian aid for them was not contained in any of those sitreps; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Continuing with the statement on the top of page 5: "We agreed with the soldiers that I would bring them a map the following day. Next day I arrived in the hamlet again and gave a map to the soldiers. I showed them a possible route to Bosnia. In two days I went to Podinarje again and found out from the local residents that the soldiers failed to get to Bosnia and returned." Now, Mr. Ermolaev, it's true that the UN, particularly the UNMOs, were supposed to be neutral and/or impartial; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And in this particular case one of your subordinates was attempting to assist combat forces in an escape to Bosnia; correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic, I think we need a proper foundation for the question. We have two matters. First that we find such a thing in the statement, and we have the question whether the witness is aware of this. Let's take it step-by-step. Were you aware of these activities as described in this statement, Mr. Ermolaev?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was not aware, and I just see it, and I mean Tchernetsky on witnessing a report as well as about what was going on while I was out of the sector. So I think that it's for the first time I see it, to answer your question, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt, but I think this next question I have really is relevant to your question as to whether or not he was aware, if I may --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Then I let you proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: P94, please, page 8. By the way, before we get to that, Mr. Ermolaev, you came back on the 25th of August, 1995; correct? You were gone for a week, from the 17th to the 25th?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know, I cannot remember exactly, I mean, the days when I returned back. That was somewhere there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If we could go to page 8, please. The second paragraph of your statement that says: "I do not remember an exact date, but in the same region some eight-nine ARSK soldiers surrendered to an UNMO team which was sent for patrolling in the Dinara area. The team was headed by the Russian UNMO A. Tchernetsky. Having received initial report from Tchernetsky from the field I moved there myself and then informed General Forand and asked for his support in hand-over procedures." Did I read that correctly, Mr. Ermolaev?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely correct. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: So you received the initial report from Mr. Tchernetsky, and you went there yourself. That is according to your statement of May 2002.

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot -- I'm just trying to recollect this particular -- my goings for patrol on this particular date, and I do think that I visited myself these villages. I do not quite remember whether I spoke with these persons or with locals. I do not exactly remember. But what I do remember, that such an intention we started immediately decide, because that was unusual and not the function of UNMO to deal with, you know, those people who'd like to surrender, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. And it wasn't UNMO's function either, was it, to provide enemy combatant forces with maps to aid them to get to Bosnia; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see it's a little bit difficult for me to comment on your question with enemy combatant forces and that UNMOs function whether or not to give them maps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Was it within your mandate, Mr. Ermolaev, the UNMO mandate, to give the ARSK force hidden somewhere in the woods maps to go into Bosnia. It's a pretty simple question, sir.

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's -- it's a bit difficult for me to explain. I want to attract attention to this fact, because first of all I --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] Mr. Ermolaev, it's pretty simple question, sir.

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I do not know, I mean, what map we're speaking about, whether it was a touristic map to show the roads, and I do believe that local populations know their local roads much better than --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ermolaev, what you're explaining to us that there was no need to give the maps because they knew the roads already which is a rather --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First of all, you were not asked for an explanation why it was useless to give them the maps, but the question was simply put to you whether giving maps, whether of any use or not, in the context of finding the way to Bosnia was within the -- within the UNMO mandate. That's the simple question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. We -- we never instructed just to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Even that is not the question whether you instructed anyone, but the first question was whether it was within the mandate.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was not within the mandate we had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] please proceed, Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't have any other questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are next.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I am next.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're next. You will now be cross-examined by Mr. Kehoe. That's -- yes. The -- even in a high-tech courtroom the logistics as far as lecterns are concerned is still complicated. You'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Kehoe who is counsel for Mr. Gotovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Ermolaev. Excuse me. I didn't put the microphone on. Good morning, Mr. Ermolaev.

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'd like to turn your attention to P99. If I can bring that on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, have we dealt with the other statement? Is that -- and I'm still looking at Mr. Kuzmanovic, the statement given by Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have we -- have you tendered the statement you earlier referred to or would you leave it to having read a portion of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to tender that portion of the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now -- one second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for reminding me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I have no objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objection. Now, we are talking about the portion, it's a bit of a --

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, just to clarify --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... a good thing to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: We will certainly be entering the entire statement into evidence through Mr. Tchernetsky.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then why not yet --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- let the entire statement, then we have the full context.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be Exhibit D152, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And for the whole of the statement did you intend to tender that under Rule 92 ter?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: We had, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll reserve the position of the Chamber in respect of if the witness would come and say, "This is not what I stated and this is not what I would repeat," then of course we would have to further deal with the matter and we might have to reconsider the admission of the whole of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D152 with this proviso is admitted into evidence. Please proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Ermolaev, I'd like to direct your attention to some days prior to Operation Storm and to some of the activities in the Cetina valley. Do you recall that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIKHAIL ERMOLAEV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. And if we could pull up P99, which is a situation report from the 23rd of July, 1995. And if we can go to page 8 of 22. Now, page 8 of 22 we have the summaries of meetings, and if you could just glance at that one for one moment, and we will get back to it.
